title: Which auction rule pays the seller most?
hook: Make the winner pay their own bid, not the runner-up's. Surely the seller earns more?

knows: second-price bidders bid their true value
doesNotKnow: that with equilibrium bidding, first-price, second-price and even all-pay auctions earn the seller the same on average

misconception: Making winners pay their own bid must earn the seller more than charging the second-highest bid.
objective: The learner can explain that each rule changes how much bidders bid, so a higher price paid by one bidder (second-price), a lower price paid by the winner (first-price) and small bids paid by everyone (all-pay) all average the same for the seller.

claims.text: In 20,000 simulated auctions the seller averages $33.4 under second-price, $33.3 under first-price and $33.3 under all-pay.
claims.source: Demo.tsx: mulberry32(97), auction i takes values 100·r() for bidder A then B; seed 97 is the brief's, not chosen by the builder for the result. Totals over 20,000: 33.395 (second-price), 33.303 (first-price, bid v/2), 33.302 (all-pay, bid v²/200). Re-run in node by the builder (ncm-e02); matches the brief's check.

claims.text: Theory gives $100 ÷ 3, about $33.3, for all three rules with two bidders and values uniform on $0 to $100: on average the seller collects the lower of the two values.
With these values, the optimal bids are: second-price, your value (the winner pays the lower value); first-price, half your value; all-pay, value squared ÷ 200, paid by both bidders.
claims.source: Symmetric equilibria for two bidders with values U(0,100): second-price truthful bidding is dominant; first-price b(v) = v/2; all-pay b(v) = v²/200 (all-pay bid = expected payment of a bidder with value v: v·(v/100) − ∫₀^v (x/100) dx = v²/200). Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 9 for first- and second-price. Fact-checker confirms.

claims.text: Each rule changes how much bidders bid, and the changes cancel, so the seller's average is the same.
claims.source: Revenue equivalence for standard auctions with independent private values: R. B. Myerson, 'Optimal auction design', Math. Oper. Res. 6 (1981); J. G. Riley and W. F. Samuelson, Am. Econ. Rev. 71 (1981); Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 9. Fact-checker confirms attribution.

claims.text: This is a model: two bidders, values independent and uniform, everyone bidding optimally.
claims.source: Lesson framing; stage chip 'Model: 2 bidders · values random $0–100 · seed 97'.

recall.question: A seller switches from second-price to first-price sealed bids. Bidders' values come from the same spread and everyone bids optimally. What happens to the seller's average revenue?
options: It rises, because the winner now pays their own bid
It stays about the same, because bidders shade their bids
recall.why: Under first-price the winner pays their own bid, but bids are shaded (half the value here), so on average the seller collects the same as charging the lower value.
